report:
**Conclusion:** Your “no” is the best overall answer—at least for *routine* use. High-quality current evidence does not show that probiotics reliably shorten acute infectious diarrhea.

The key 2020 Cochrane review found that probiotics probably make little or no difference in diarrhea persisting ≥48 hours and concluded that it is uncertain whether they shorten time to recovery. Earlier trials often suggested a modest reduction in duration, but results varied substantially; when analyses emphasized the larger, lower-risk-of-bias trials, the apparent benefit was not supported.  
https://www.cochrane.org/CD003048/INFECTN_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/

Why there is still disagreement: “probiotics” are not one treatment—effects, if any, may depend on the exact strain, dose, population, pathogen, and setting. The American Gastroenterological Association therefore *suggests against* probiotics for children with acute infectious gastroenteritis (conditional recommendation; moderate-quality evidence).  
https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext

In contrast, ESPGHAN says clinicians *may* use certain named strains (including **Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus** GG) in children, but explicitly grades the evidence for reduced diarrhea duration as **low certainty**. This is not support for generic over-the-counter probiotic products.  
https://www.espghan.org/dam/jcr:299e3330-b1b6-4940-aa72-786501bffff1/2023_Probiotics+for+the+Management+of+Pediatric+Gastrointestinal+Disorders:+Position+Paper+of+the+ESPGHAN+Special+Interest+Group+on+Gut+Microbiota+and+Modifications.pdf

Oral rehydration remains the proven priority; seek care promptly for dehydration, bloody stool, high fever, severe pain, or concerning illness in an infant, older adult, or immunocompromised person.
